q: To be an effective teacher in this day and age, you’ve got to be mentally tough.
Slow your body and your mind will follow. If you’re swayed by the pull of your phone, then you’ll likely be more easily swayed by your students.
According to research, the pain of cold showers triggers chemicals in the brain that counteract the discomfort, leaving you calmer and happier for hours afterward.
The mental strength comes from delaying gratification, which has been shown to correlate with success.

t: Break the Spell of the Tell
q: Team leaders push, prod, and cajole people to get them to act. Yet, people wait for instructions.
For leaders, TELL is the faster and most efficient way to get others to do what you want them to.
Leaders who vacillate between directing others and then giving them the freedom to act on their own confuse everyone
Breaking the pattern of TELL requires a tremendous amount of patience on everyone’s part.
Stepping back and watching people execute can be tremendously painful.
Once deprogrammed from the TELL, people regain the ability to act on their own, without waiting for instructions.

t: How To Become A Better Teacher Instantly
q: It’s to take responsibility for everything that happens in your classroom. Ownership. Duty. Blame. Onus. The buck stops with me. The whole nine.
Take responsibility anyway. For it all. It can be the best teaching decision you’ve ever made. As soon as you do it, as soon as you say, “It’s on me,” things will instantly begin to change.
You’ll stop complaining and being a victim. You’ll instead automatically look for solutions. Your disposition and character will also change.

Taking responsibility is leadership. Not many people are willing to do it because it’s hard and takes toughness. You have to stand on your own two feet, embrace uncertainty, and risk the fear of excellence .
Do it now before the start of a new school year. It’s a decision, nothing more. Go on. Walk to the edge. Close your eyes. And take the leap.
x: Taking full ownership of everything that happens in the classroom, regardless of circumstance, is framed as an instantly transformational decision.
Students remain responsible for their own behavior, but the teacher benefits from taking responsibility for outcomes anyway.
Linsin presents a single, uncomfortable but transformational idea.
Taking responsibility is described as an act of leadership requiring the courage to abandon excuses and risk uncertainty.
The piece closes with an extended metaphor of leaping off a ledge, urging readers to make the decision immediately, before the new school year begins.

t: 3 Misconceptions Of Effective Classroom Management anagement/
q: The only thing that needs to be strict is your adherence to your classroom management plan. As for where you place your boundaries, it’s up to you.
The idea that you have to be hard and severe while managing your classroom endures to this day. The truth is, a stern disposition is a waste of energy.
Good classroom management happens fast if you follow the core principles of SCM . Your confidence in what you’re doing is enough to communicate that your class is different.
When you set your behavior expectations in highly specific detail, whereby students feel the shock of excellence, they sit up straighter. They desire to be better.
You can and should expect impeccable behavior right now . There is no warming up. There is no room for doubt or excuses.
x: He clarifies that what needs to be strict is a teacher's adherence to their own plan, not the severity of the boundaries themselves, which can be set flexibly to match a teacher's preferences.

Effective classroom management does not require a long runway.

t: Autonomous Text, Autonomous Literacy, Autonomous Humanity
q: The “banking model” of education, however, served me well as conceptual metaphor and then expanded to the “factory model,” a controlled systematic model with a conveyor belt equipped to separate and segregate substandard products. The system served the oppressor and guaranteed a pliant population.

Within a few years I would augment my emerging understanding with a third side to the triangle: Power, Hegemony, Literacy. Brian Street, whom I came to read in courses at UC Davis in the mid-1980s, distinguished between an “autonomous” model and an “ideological” model of literacy.

Seen as a free-standing, self-contained, technical human app one perfects through proper training, available in all known languages, once installed in the brain, autonomous literacy operates generically much like breathing, a machine with an on-off switch one learns to use at a high level regardless of context, intention, historical formation, or shared values and beliefs. Teachers assign, students read, teacher talks, students test. Bank accounts swell.

School literacy in the Western world is a collection of literacy practices shaping events electrified with life-altering power. Assigning a text to a student to read is not a straightforward matter of assigning the task of decoding the words and requiring a standardized mental model of its meaning.

Embedding assignments in contexts of academic power changes everything. School language is privileged; reading to pass tests or to demonstrate knowledge becomes a habit of mind. Ways of reading and writing, whole genres of reading and writing, are delegitimized. Knowledge is a predefined commodity legitimated by a credentialed professional.
Thus, education and power are terms of an indissoluble couplet. It is at times of social upheaval that this relationship between education and power becomes most visible (p.46).
x: The banking and factory models of schooling serve the powerful and produce a pliant population.
Street's autonomous model treats literacy as a neutral, portable skill, while the ideological model sees it as practice shaped by power.
Underwood frames reading failure among students as political and socially reproduced, not merely technical or phonological.
Assigning a text in school is never a simple decoding task, because academic power shapes which language and genres count as legitimate.

Underwood applies this to school literacy, where school language is privileged, other ways of reading and writing are delegitimized, and knowledge is a commodity validated by credentialed professionals.
He ties curricular control, including recent state legislation, to Apple's claim that education and power are an indissoluble couplet.

t: Jim Experiences Learning to Read as an Adult
q: Unfortunately, Jim enjoyed none of the advantages but all of the disadvantages of ability grouping in reading. He carried indelibly in his metaphors his feelings about being in the bad reading group.

Within a few weeks Jim had picked up some phonics skills. He discovered residual learning stuck somewhere in his brain, surprising himself with how much he could do with help. He was excited about his progress.
Let’s make it ‘the.’ So I would write tttt, you know, 75 times or a hunnert times, hhhh it didn’t matter to me because I figured I wasn’t going to learn to spell that way. Big deal, writin’ it down.

Jim remembered being left out in the cold in high school. The logic of the factory metaphor—the famous factory model of education—must have forced the urban school district to allocate finite resources according to principle of efficiency. As children got older, those with the least—or no—chance of profiting from reading instruction were removed from remediation to make room for those with a better chance.

Jim credited his tutor’s consistent focus on monitoring him and making him do the work of turning print into speech as key to his development. If I had been more on the ball forty years ago, I would have asked to observe a tutoring session. He also praised the Laubach materials.

I had been reading and rereading Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed for about a year at the time, keeping a reflective journal, and noted that Jim was on the cusp of a milestone: When the oppressed pivot from asking “How do I read?” to asking, “Why was I not taught to read?” the pedagogy is taking.

The core finding had staying power. Whether you agree with the conceptual framework of the APL regarding what behaviors count as evidence of “functional illiteracy,” the published finding that “21.7% of American adults are functionally illiterate” became the default position.
x: Jim's schooling shows how ability grouping and special-education tracking can stop a child's reading development while appearing to serve him.
Jim's adult progress came from a tutor who built a human connection first, then used explicit phonics and made him decode words himself.
Rote punishment spelling (write it 25, 50, then 100 times) produced shortcuts and disengagement rather than learning to spell.
Underwood reads this through the factory model of education, in which finite remediation resources were withdrawn from the children least likely to profit.
The tutoring succeeds because it combines a human connection, explicit phonics, and a tutor who refuses to supply words and makes Jim do the work of turning print into speech.
Terry Underwood revisits a decades-old interview with Jim, a janitor who is learning to read as an adult through a volunteer Laubach phonics tutor at the public library.

t: A Simple Way To Have Better Classroom Management Next Year
q: The way it works is to list the five most disruptive, annoying , and stressful misbehaviors you witnessed last school year.
Now, draw a line from each misbehavior to the rule it breaks. If you can’t do this, then you need to create another rule.
You see, whatever misbehavior you model—as in how not to behave —you’re less likely to get from your students.

It communicates in a way students understand why such misbehavior is wrong and how it tramples on the rights of others. In fact, if modeled explicitly and followed by your promise to hold your students accountable, they’re loathe to repeat it.

And because it comes at the beginning of the year, before they can engage in such behavior, they won’t be offended. You’re not poking fun at anyone personally. However, many will see themselves in the behavior.
x: A quick end-of-year exercise: list the five most disruptive misbehaviors from the past year and match each to an existing classroom rule, adding new rules as needed.

Modeling misbehavior with some exaggeration highlights its absurdity in a way students understand and remember.
